name: Expensify
tagline: Receipt capture, cards, reimbursements, travel, invoices, and accounting sync

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.name: Personal
tiers.limits: Unlimited SmartScans; unlimited manual expenses and mileage; CSV export; 0 workspace categories, tags, accounting integrations, or Expensify Card controls

tiers.name: Collect, pay per use
tiers.limits: $5 per unique member used in a month; expense reports, reimbursements, cards, travel, invoicing, and accounting sync
tiers.notes: Current new-customer model; no annual commitment required.

tiers.name: Control, pay per use
tiers.limits: $36 per active member in a month; advanced approvals, compliance, controls, and accounting features

tiers.name: Control, annual commitment
tiers.limits: $18 per committed member/month; active members above the commitment are $36 each
tiers.notes: Expensify Card usage can reduce the included rate as low as $9 and overage as low as $18.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Unlimited SmartScans, manual expenses, mileage, and CSV export for personal use; 0 workspace categories/tags, accounting integrations, or card administration
pricing.billingTerms: pay-per-use monthly plans; optional 12-month Control commitment billed monthly
pricing.hiddenCosts: A 12-month commitment can be increased but not decreased during the term; active users over the committed count cost $36 each. The maximum 50% card discount depends on the share of approved USD expenses put on the Expensify Card. Taxes may be added. Legacy subscriptions predating April 1, 2025 can use different $10/$5 structures.

verdictSummary: Do not mistake the interface for the product. Expensify's durable value is banking, compliance, trust, which a solo one-shot build cannot reproduce responsibly. The prompt therefore builds only the closest honest personal consolation tool.
coreLoopDIY: Build a private expense management ledger that imports user-supplied CSV files, categorizes entries, reconciles balances, and exports reports.
diyTimeEstimate: not a true replacement; consolation build in one to two days
replacementScope: consolation build only; the paid product's moat remains
requirements: CSV exports from the user's own accounts
Explicit README warning that this is a consolation build, not a production replacement
whatYouLose: bank, payment, tax, and reconciliation integrations
live bank feeds and payment rails
whyPeopleStillPay: Expensify: People pay because errors touch real money. Bank connections, reconciliation, tax changes, evidence, security, and support are the product.
ongoingBurden: Own data integrity, backups, import mapping, reconciliation, security, audit logs, tax changes, and recovery.

rejectedAlternatives.desc: Free for three users, but corporate cards, direct reimbursements and travel booking live on paid plans.

notes: Credibility row: Expensify survives for a structural reason, not because its interface is difficult to copy.
prompt:
Build the closest honest consolation tool inspired by Expensify; do not claim to replace its structural moat.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a private expense management ledger that imports user-supplied CSV files, categorizes entries, reconciles balances, and exports reports.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: tax and accounting rule updates; audited security and recovery; multi-user controls and accountant workflows.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
